history.hpi: Patient reports feeling lightheaded and 'fuzzy' after standing up from the couch, then has no memory of the fall itself; daughter states she was unresponsive for approximately 10 seconds before regaining consciousness. Patient now complains of generalized weakness and mild chest heaviness. Denies prior syncope, chest pain, or shortness of breath prior to the event.
history.events: Stood up from the couch, became lightheaded, and collapsed to the floor; daughter witnessed the fall and called 911 immediately

scene.dispatch: Medic 4, respond to 1420 Birchwood Lane for a 74-year-old female, syncope, patient now conscious but weak.
scene.location: Private residence, living room; patient found seated in a chair with family assistance after a witnessed collapse
scene.safety: Scene safe, family present and cooperative
scene.bystanders: Daughter witnessed patient stand up, go pale, and collapse to the floor; no seizure activity noted, brief loss of consciousness approximately 10 seconds
visualCues: Patient pale and diaphoretic, seated in a chair with family assistance
Small abrasion to forehead from the fall
Medication bottles visible on the kitchen counter (metoprolol, digoxin, levothyroxine)

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: 74-year-old female found post-syncopal episode, now awake but pale, diaphoretic, and weak. Initial vitals reveal profound bradycardia (HR 32) with hypotension (78/50), consistent with symptomatic bradycardia requiring immediate assessment and monitoring.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Slightly labored, symmetric chest rise, no accessory muscle use
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse weak and slow, palpable at approximately 32/min; skin pale and diaphoretic
otherFindings: Small forehead abrasion from fall, no active bleeding
Reports generalized weakness and mild chest heaviness
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: I just felt so dizzy when I stood up... I don't really remember falling.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply cardiac monitor and obtain 12-lead EKG
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Additional Evaluation: Cardiac monitoring; Oxygen saturation (SPO2); Ongoing vital signs; 12-lead EKG; Blood glucose level (BGL)
expectedActions.rationale: Identifies the underlying rhythm (third-degree AV block) driving the symptomatic bradycardia and rules out ACS as a contributing cause.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult and Pediatric Syncope and Near Syncope

expectedActions.shortAction: Administer oxygen titrated to a target SpO2 of 94-98%
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Administer oxygen as appropriate with a target of achieving 94–98% saturation
expectedActions.rationale: Corrects hypoxia as a contributing cause of bradycardia per protocol treatment goals.

expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Check blood glucose and treat hypoglycemia per the Hypoglycemia Guideline and Hyperglycemia Guideline
expectedActions.rationale: Rules out hypoglycemia as a reversible cause of altered perfusion/bradycardia.
Required for atropine and any subsequent vasopressor or sedation administration.

expectedActions.shortAction: Atropine 1 mg IV push; may repeat every 3-5 minutes to a max total dose of 3 mg
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Atropine 1 mg IV q 3–5 minutes (maximum total dose of 3 mg)
expectedActions.rationale: First-line additional therapy for symptomatic bradycardia per protocol.

transitions.condition: IV access obtained and initial assessment complete; heart rate remains 32 with hypotension (78/50), meeting inclusion criteria for symptomatic bradycardia requiring pharmacologic treatment.

phases.name: Atropine given
phases.description: IV access is established and the patient remains symptomatic with HR 32 and hypotension. Per protocol, atropine is the first-line additional therapy for symptomatic bradycardia.
phases.triggerCondition: IV access obtained; heart rate remains 32 with hypotension (BP 78/50) meeting inclusion criteria for symptomatic bradycardia; atropine is indicated as the first additional therapy per protocol.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse weak and slow, IV established in left AC
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: I still feel really weak and lightheaded.

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess HR and BP after each atropine dose; recognize third-degree block may be atropine-refractory
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Third-degree heart block or the denervated heart (as in cardiac transplant) may not respond to atropine and in these cases, proceed quickly to chronotropic agents (such as epinephrine or dopamine) or transcutaneous pacing
expectedActions.rationale: Prevents delay in escalating to pacing when atropine is unlikely to work for infranodal (third-degree) block.

expectedActions.shortAction: Administer sedation/analgesia prior to pacing per local protocol
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If pacing is performed, consider sedation or pain control
expectedActions.rationale: TCP is painful; sedation improves patient tolerance and cooperation.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply pacing pads (anterior/posterior) and initiate transcutaneous pacing
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Transcutaneous Pacing – If pacing is performed, consider sedation or pain control
expectedActions.rationale: Third-degree block is atropine-refractory; TCP is the next escalation per protocol.

transitions.condition: Two 1 mg doses of atropine (2 mg total) administered IV with no improvement in heart rate or blood pressure; patient remains symptomatic with HR 32 and BP 76/48. Provider recognizes atropine-refractory third-degree block and escalates to transcutaneous pacing.
Atropine given to the maximum total dose of 3 mg without initiating transcutaneous pacing; heart rate remains 32 and blood pressure continues to fall, with worsening mental status.

Transcutaneous pacing is initiated without administering sedation or analgesia; patient experiences significant pain and agitation from pacing, complicating capture assessment and patient cooperation.

phases.name: TCP initiated
phases.description: Atropine has failed to improve the patient's heart rate or blood pressure. Per protocol, in cases of impending hemodynamic collapse the provider proceeds directly to transcutaneous pacing, with sedation or pain control considered.
phases.triggerCondition: After 2 mg atropine IV with no improvement in heart rate or blood pressure, patient remains symptomatic with HR 32 and BP 76/48. Per protocol, in cases of impending hemodynamic collapse, proceed directly to transcutaneous pacing.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse weak and slow, worsening pallor
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: What are you about to do to me? I'm scared.

expectedActions.shortAction: Confirm electrical and mechanical capture; document pacer rate, mA, and patient response
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Pacing: Time started or stopped, rate, joules, capture, and response rate
expectedActions.rationale: Mechanical capture (palpable pulse matching paced rate) confirms effective pacing, not just electrical spikes on the monitor.

transitions.condition: Pacing pads applied, sedation administered, and transcutaneous pacing captures at the set rate with a palpable pulse; heart rate rises to the paced rate and blood pressure improves.

phases.name: Capture achieved; perfusion improved
phases.description: Transcutaneous pacing successfully captures with sedation on board. Heart rate rises to the paced rate and blood pressure improves; the patient is less pale and more comfortable. Ongoing reassessment and transport preparation continue.
phases.triggerCondition: Transcutaneous pacing captures at the set rate with sedation on board; heart rate rises to the paced rate and blood pressure improves, patient less pale and more comfortable.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse strong, regular, matching paced rate
otherFindings: Pacer capture confirmed with palpable femoral pulse matching monitor rate
Sedation on board, patient calm and cooperative
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: That feels a lot better. Is it working now?

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess vitals and mental status; provide advance hospital notification given persistent hemodynamic instability requiring pacing
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Provide advanced notification to the hospital
expectedActions.rationale: Ensures receiving facility is prepared for a paced, previously unstable bradycardia patient.

expectedActions.shortAction: Continue cardiac monitoring and reassess vitals throughout transport
expectedActions.rationale: Third-degree block can recur or the patient may lose capture; ongoing monitoring detects deterioration early.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult and Pediatric Syncope and Near Syncope

phases.name: Atropine repeated, pacing delayed
phases.description: Atropine is repeated to the maximum total dose of 3 mg without initiating transcutaneous pacing. The third-degree block does not respond, and the patient's perfusion continues to deteriorate.
phases.triggerCondition: Atropine given to the maximum total dose of 3 mg without initiating transcutaneous pacing; heart rate remains 32 and blood pressure falls further, with worsening mental status approaching unresponsiveness.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse weak, thready, slow; peripheral pulses difficult to palpate

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize impending hemodynamic collapse; proceed directly to transcutaneous pacing without further atropine
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: In cases of impending hemodynamic collapse, proceed directly to transcutaneous pacing
expectedActions.rationale: Further atropine at max dose provides no additional benefit for third-degree block; delaying pacing risks cardiovascular collapse.

phases.name: Pacing without sedation
phases.description: Transcutaneous pacing is initiated without prior sedation or analgesia. The patient experiences significant pain and agitation from the pacing current, complicating assessment of capture and patient cooperation.
phases.triggerCondition: Transcutaneous pacing initiated without administering sedation or analgesia; patient experiences significant pain and agitation from pacing, complicating capture assessment and patient cooperation.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse strong, matching paced rate, but patient thrashing
otherFindings: Patient grimacing and guarding chest wall with each pacing spike
Difficult to obtain accurate capture assessment due to patient movement
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: Stop, stop, that hurts! Please stop!

expectedActions.shortAction: Administer sedation/analgesia promptly to reduce pain and improve tolerance of pacing
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If pacing is performed, consider sedation or pain control
expectedActions.rationale: Untreated pain from TCP causes patient distress and can obscure accurate assessment of mechanical capture.
